# Objectives

In this exercise you will apply the whole co-kriging workflow of Examples 3.1 and 3.2 to a new pair of variables:

- Predict the concentration of **cadmium** (primary variable) in the Meuse study area using **copper** (secondary variable).
- Compare **ordinary kriging** (cadmium only) and **ordinary co-kriging** (cadmium and copper) using prediction maps, their standard errors and cross-validation.
- Analyse when co-kriging is worthwhile.

# Packages

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(gstat)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
```

# Description of the data

We use again the `meuse` dataset (155 soil samples) and the `meuse.grid` prediction grid (3103 nodes).

- **Cadmium** (`cadmium`, ppm) is a highly toxic heavy metal, which accumulates in soils and can be taken up by crops.
- **Copper** (`copper`, ppm) comes from the same industrial sources and, like lead and zinc, is transported by the river floods. It is measured on the same soil samples as cadmium.

```{r}
data(meuse, package="sp")         # soil samples
data(meuse.grid, package="sp")    # prediction grid

meuse_sf <- meuse |>
  as_tibble() |>
  st_as_sf(coords=c("x","y"), crs=28992)

grid_sf <- meuse.grid |>
  as_tibble() |>
  st_as_sf(coords=c("x","y"), crs=28992)
```

In the first part of the exercise, both variables are available at all 155 locations:

```{r}
cd_sf <- meuse_sf    # primary variable: cadmium (155 samples)
cu_sf <- meuse_sf    # secondary variable: copper (155 samples)
```

# Tasks

## Exploratory analysis

Plot the histograms of cadmium and copper, both on the original and on the log scale, and compute the correlation between both variables.

- Which scale is more appropriate for the analysis?
- Is copper a promising secondary variable to predict cadmium?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
hist(cd_sf$cadmium, main = "Cadmium", xlab = "ppm", col = "grey80")
hist(cd_sf$copper, main = "Copper", xlab = "ppm", col = "grey80")
hist(log(cd_sf$cadmium), main = "log(Cadmium)", xlab = "log(ppm)", col = "grey80")
hist(log(cd_sf$copper), main = "log(Copper)", xlab = "log(ppm)", col = "grey80")

cor(cd_sf$cadmium, cd_sf$copper)
cor(log(cd_sf$cadmium), log(cd_sf$copper))
```
- As with lead and zinc, both variables are very right-skewed, and the log transformation makes their distributions more symmetric. We will work on the **log scale**.
- The correlation between both variables on the log scale is high (`r round(cor(log(cd_sf$cadmium), log(cd_sf$copper)), 2)`), so copper is a promising secondary variable. However, it is lower than the correlation between lead and zinc (0.97).
:::
:::

## Semivariogram of the primary variable

Compute the empirical semivariogram of `log(cadmium)` and fit a spherical model with a nugget effect. Choose the initial values by visual inspection of the empirical semivariogram.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
v_cd <- variogram(log(cadmium) ~ 1, cd_sf)
vgm_cd <- fit.variogram(v_cd, model=vgm(psill=1.5, model="Sph",
                                        range=1000, nugget=0.5))
vgm_cd

plot(v_cd, vgm_cd, pch = 19,
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     main = "Semivariogram of log-cadmium (Cd)")
```

- Nugget effect $\approx$ `r round(vgm_cd$psill[1], 2)`, partial sill $\approx$ `r round(vgm_cd$psill[2], 2)` and range $\approx$ `r round(vgm_cd$range[2])` m.
- The nugget effect represents about `r round(100 * vgm_cd$psill[1] / sum(vgm_cd$psill))`% of the total sill, much more than for lead: cadmium shows more variability at very short distances.
:::
:::

## Linear model of coregionalization

Create a `gstat` object with both variables, compute the direct and cross empirical semivariograms and fit a linear model of coregionalization.

- Is the cross-semivariogram structured?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
g <- gstat(NULL, id = "Cd", formula = log(cadmium) ~ 1, data = cd_sf)
g <- gstat(g,    id = "Cu", formula = log(copper) ~ 1,  data = cu_sf)

v <- variogram(g)
lmc <- fit.lmc(v, g, model=vgm_cd)
lmc$model
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6

plot(v, lmc, pch = 19, col = "black",
     xlab = "Distance (m)", ylab = "Semivariance",
     scales = list(alternating = 1, tck = c(1, 0)))
```

The cross-semivariogram increases with distance and levels off at about `r round(sum(lmc$model$Cd.Cu$psill), 2)`: there is a clear **spatial correlation** between cadmium and copper.
:::
:::

## Predictions

Predict cadmium on the `meuse.grid` nodes using ordinary kriging and co-kriging. Plot the predictions and their standard errors for both methods.

- Are there differences between both methods?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
pred_krig <- krige(log(cadmium) ~ 1, cd_sf, grid_sf, model=vgm_cd, debug.level=0)
pred_cokrig <- predict(lmc, grid_sf, debug.level=0)

pred_sf <- grid_sf |>
  mutate(krig_pred   = pred_krig$var1.pred,
         krig_sd     = sqrt(pred_krig$var1.var),
         cokrig_pred = pred_cokrig$Cd.pred,
         cokrig_sd   = sqrt(pred_cokrig$Cd.var)) |>
  st_buffer(dist=20, endCapStyle="SQUARE")
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

tmap_mode("plot")

# Predictions
tm_shape(pred_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("krig_pred", "cokrig_pred"),
              fill.scale  = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "log(cadmium)"),
              fill.free = FALSE,    # common colour scale
              col = NULL) +         # no cell borders
  tm_facets_wrap(nrow=1) +
  tm_layout(panel.labels = c("Ordinary kriging", "Co-kriging"))

# Standard errors
tm_shape(pred_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = c("krig_sd", "cokrig_sd"),
              fill.scale  = tm_scale_continuous(values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "SD (log scale)"),
              fill.free = FALSE,
              col = NULL) +
  tm_facets_wrap(nrow=1) +
  tm_layout(panel.labels = c("Ordinary kriging", "Co-kriging"))
```

- Both prediction maps are very similar.
- The standard errors of co-kriging are only slightly lower: the median standard error decreases from `r round(median(pred_sf$krig_sd), 3)` to `r round(median(pred_sf$cokrig_sd), 3)`.
:::
:::

## Cross-validation

Compare both methods using leave-one-out cross-validation. Compute the mean absolute error (MAE) and the root mean squared error (RMSE). Plot the observed values against the cross-validation predictions for both methods.

- Does co-kriging improve on ordinary kriging?
- Why is the improvement so small, if the correlation between cadmium and copper is high?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
# Ordinary kriging
cv_krig <- krige.cv(log(cadmium) ~ 1, cd_sf, model=vgm_cd, nfold=nrow(cd_sf),
                    debug.level=0)

# Co-kriging
cv_cokrig <- gstat.cv(lmc, nfold=nrow(cd_sf), remove.all=TRUE, debug.level=0)

cv_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Ordinary kriging", "Co-kriging"),
  MAE    = c(mean(abs(cv_krig$residual)), mean(abs(cv_cokrig$residual))),
  RMSE   = c(sqrt(mean(cv_krig$residual^2)), sqrt(mean(cv_cokrig$residual^2)))
)
cv_results |> mutate(across(c(MAE, RMSE), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5

lims <- range(c(cv_krig$observed, cv_krig$var1.pred, cv_cokrig$Cd.pred))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(cv_krig$var1.pred, cv_krig$observed, pch = 19, xlim = lims, ylim = lims,
     xlab = "Predicted (cross-validation)", ylab = "Observed",
     main = "Ordinary kriging")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "red")
plot(cv_cokrig$Cd.pred, cv_cokrig$observed, pch = 19, xlim = lims, ylim = lims,
     xlab = "Predicted (cross-validation)", ylab = "Observed",
     main = "Co-kriging")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

- Co-kriging slightly reduces both errors (the RMSE decreases from `r sprintf("%.3f", cv_results$RMSE[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", cv_results$RMSE[2])`), but the improvement is **very small**. The observed vs. predicted plots are also almost identical.
- The reason is that both variables have been measured at the **same locations**: wherever copper is available, cadmium is also available, so copper provides almost no new spatial information. A high correlation is not enough: co-kriging is most useful when the secondary variable has been observed at many more locations than the primary variable.
:::
:::

# Optional: cadmium observed at 50 locations

To reproduce the typical situation of co-kriging, assume that cadmium has only been measured at a random subset of 50 samples, while copper is still available at all 155 locations:

```{r}
set.seed(123)
idx <- sample(nrow(meuse_sf), 50)

cd_sf <- meuse_sf |> slice(idx)   # primary variable: 50 samples
cu_sf <- meuse_sf                 # secondary variable: 155 samples
```

Repeat the semivariogram analysis and the cross-validation comparison (maps are not needed). Note that:

- With this sampling design, the zero-distance lag must be removed from the empirical semivariograms before fitting the linear model of coregionalization (see Example 3.2).
- If the co-kriging step returns the error `variograms do not satisfy a legal model`, fit the linear model of coregionalization with the argument `fit.lmc(..., correct.diagonal = 1.01)`.

- Does co-kriging improve on ordinary kriging now?
- Compare the results with those obtained with the 155 samples.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{r}
# Ordinary kriging
v_cd_50 <- variogram(log(cadmium) ~ 1, cd_sf)
vgm_cd_50 <- fit.variogram(v_cd_50, model=vgm(psill=1.5, model="Sph",
                                              range=1000, nugget=0.5))
cv_krig_50 <- krige.cv(log(cadmium) ~ 1, cd_sf, model=vgm_cd_50, nfold=nrow(cd_sf),
                       debug.level=0)

# Co-kriging
g_50 <- gstat(NULL, id = "Cd", formula = log(cadmium) ~ 1, data = cd_sf)
g_50 <- gstat(g_50, id = "Cu", formula = log(copper) ~ 1,  data = cu_sf)
v_50 <- variogram(g_50) |> filter(dist > 0)    # remove the zero-distance lag
lmc_50 <- fit.lmc(v_50, g_50, model=vgm_cd_50, correct.diagonal=1.01)
cv_cokrig_50 <- gstat.cv(lmc_50, nfold=nrow(cd_sf), remove.all=TRUE, debug.level=0)

cv_results_50 <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Ordinary kriging", "Co-kriging"),
  MAE    = c(mean(abs(cv_krig_50$residual)), mean(abs(cv_cokrig_50$residual))),
  RMSE   = c(sqrt(mean(cv_krig_50$residual^2)), sqrt(mean(cv_cokrig_50$residual^2)))
)
```

::: {.callout-note title="The argument `correct.diagonal = 1.01`"}
The sills fitted by `fit.lmc()` must satisfy the condition $|b_{12}| \le \sqrt{b_{11}\,b_{22}}$ for each basic structure. With this subsample, the fitted sills of the spherical structure lie exactly on the limit of this condition, and `gstat` rejects the model when predicting. The argument `correct.diagonal = 1.01` multiplies the sills of the direct semivariograms by 1.01, so that the condition is strictly satisfied.
:::

::: {style="width: fit-content;"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Method  = cv_results$Method,
    MAE_155 = sprintf("%.3f", cv_results$MAE),    RMSE_155 = sprintf("%.3f", cv_results$RMSE),
    MAE_50  = sprintf("%.3f", cv_results_50$MAE), RMSE_50  = sprintf("%.3f", cv_results_50$RMSE)
  ),
  col.names = c("Method", "MAE", "RMSE", "MAE", "RMSE"),
  align = "lrrrr",
  caption = "Cross-validation results with cadmium observed at all 155 locations (columns 2-3) and at 50 locations (columns 4-5)."
)
```
:::

- With only 50 cadmium samples, co-kriging **clearly improves** on ordinary kriging: the RMSE decreases from `r sprintf("%.3f", cv_results_50$RMSE[1])` to `r sprintf("%.3f", cv_results_50$RMSE[2])` (a reduction of about `r round(100 * (1 - cv_results_50$RMSE[2] / cv_results_50$RMSE[1]))`%).
- Now copper provides information at 105 locations where cadmium is unknown, which is exactly the situation where co-kriging is worthwhile.
- The errors are larger than with 155 samples, because the semivariogram and the predictions are based on fewer cadmium observations.
- These results depend on the random subsample: with other seeds, the improvement may be larger or smaller (and occasionally co-kriging may even be slightly worse).
:::
:::
